activities.caption: guess the free satellite's resolution and rhythm
activities.name: agSentinelEstimate

config.prompt: Sentinel-2 imagery is free to everyone. What ground resolution does it deliver?
config.why: About 10-metre pixels on a roughly 5-day revisit — good enough to monitor the whole season. Drones fly centimetre resolution on demand for spot verification.
config.context: Ten metres: coarse enough to see a field, fine enough to see a zone.

activities.anchor: Imagery shows where; probes show when
activities.caption: pair each instrument with the question it answers
activities.name: agInstrumentMatch

config.prompt: Each layer of the precision stack answers a different question. Match them:

pairs.right: what did this zone actually produce — the ground truth everything else is calibrated against
where is the canopy reflecting like a stressed one
what is the soil chemistry, at a price that still makes sense

config.why: The index only flags where the canopy reflects like a stressed one — nitrogen deficiency, water stress, disease and compaction can paint the same patch. That is why the professional stack fuses imagery with yield maps, soil samples and probes.

activities.caption: put the compaction damage on the scale
activities.name: agTrafficPlace

config.prompt: Controlled traffic farming confines every wheel to permanent tramlines. Roughly what share of the field never gets driven on?
config.why: The ~80–90% of the field that never carries a wheel. Compaction alone costs double-digit yield percentages on trafficked soil, so keeping the damage to 15% of the area is a yield strategy, not just a comfort.

activities.caption: true or false — the see-and-spray trade
activities.name: agPrecisionJudge

statements.s: Auto-steer was an adoption leader because its payoff needs no agronomy.
statements.why: Eliminating pass overlap saves about 5–10% of fuel and input directly.

statements.s: See-and-spray cuts herbicide volumes 50–90% per pass in commercial deployments.
statements.why: Cameras trigger nozzles individually. The resistance-management dividend may matter more than the savings.

statements.s: The yield-maximising nitrogen rate is the right rate to apply.
statements.why: The right rate maximises profit, not yield, and by construction sits below the yield peak.

statements.s: A model validated in Iowa can be carried over to Punjab unchanged.
statements.why: Climate, soils and cultivars differ — the generalisation question dominates the research literature.

activities.anchor: bought about USD 18 of grain for USD 36 of fertiliser
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this prescription arithmetic
activities.name: agPrescriptionSpot

config.prompt: A student works a zone's nitrogen prescription. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Each zone gets its own response curve, from randomised strip trials of seed and N rates.
The economic optimum is where the value of the marginal yield jump just exceeds the marginal cost of the nutrient.
In the worked example the economic optimum is 220 kg/ha, about 30 kg/ha above the agronomic maximum.
The final 30 kg/ha bought about USD 18 of grain for USD 36 of fertiliser — pure loss.
So the prescription runs at the profit-maximising rate, strictly below the yield peak.
config.correction: The economic optimum of 220 kg/ha sits about 30 kg/ha BELOW the agronomic maximum, not above it.
config.why: Marginal analysis always lands below the yield peak: past the economic optimum each kilogram costs more than the grain it returns. The final 30 kg bought USD 18 of grain for USD 36 of fertiliser.

activities.caption: rebuild the timeline in instruments
activities.name: agTimelineOrder

config.prompt: Put the precision-agriculture decades in order:
items: 1980s — the first grain-flow yield sensors and grid soil sampling are prototyped
1990s — civilian GPS goes fully operational (1995) and the first variable-rate controllers follow
2000s — RTK networks spread, auto-steer industrialises, yield monitors become standard
2010s — cloud farm platforms, free Sentinel imagery from 2015, the first ag-tech investment wave
2020s — commercial see-and-spray and factory autonomous tractors
config.why: The pattern across all four decades: a military or space technology, commoditised, becomes agricultural infrastructure within a generation — and each new infrastructure monetises the previous one's data.

activities.caption: decide inside the data question
activities.name: agDataBranch

config.root: Your farm runs on one vendor's platform: their sensors, their prescriptions, their input shop. They offer a discount if you let them aggregate your yield data with your neighbours'.

start.text: The data is your farm's ground truth — and taking the discount hands it to the party that already sells you the inputs.

choices.label: Take the discount — the savings are real and immediate
choices.feedback: The prescription and the input purchase are now the same vendor, and the aggregation term is not one you negotiate.

choices.label: Ask for data portability before signing anything
choices.feedback: Who owns the yield map, and can the farmer leave the platform with their own data, are the governance terms that matter.

discount.text: You are now negotiating next year's rates against a counterparty who holds every zone's response curve you ever measured.

portable.text: You can move platforms with your own history intact — the exit option that keeps the vendor honest over a decade.

config.why: Precision agriculture's current reality is decision support with mechanical execution: sensors and algorithms find patterns and compute rates, while human agronomic judgement still owns the interpretation. The quiet antitrust question — data ownership — will shape the field as much as any sensor.

activities.caption: bet on the smallholder route
activities.name: agSmallholderPredict

config.q: Most of the world's farms are small. How does precision agriculture actually reach them?
choices: Each smallholder buys a yield-monitored combine and an RTK subscription
Through cooperative machinery, drone spray-as-a-service contractors, and phone advisories on free satellite data
It does not reach them at all — precision agriculture is structurally a large-farm technology
Through government-built variable-rate planters distributed free
config.why: The developmental version of precision agriculture is less a tractor and more a subscription: the same NDVI physics, delivered as a weekly text message.

activities.caption: fill the ratios — the grammar of selection
activities.name: agMendelCloze

config.text: Cross two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) and the F2 genotypes come out 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. If A is dominant the phenotypes collapse to a visible %%0%% : 1. In the wheat example, selfing the uniform F1 gives three quarters susceptible and %%1%% quarter resistant — and because resistance is recessive, each candidate must be genotyped to find its carriers.
config.hint: Dominance hides the heterozygotes: add the 1 AA and the 2 Aa together and compare with the 1 aa. For the second blank, the recessive phenotype is the smallest class.

activities.anchor: does not mean stronger, fitter, or more common in the
activities.caption: true or false — what dominance actually says
activities.name: agDominanceJudge

statements.s: Dominance describes what happens to the phenotype when both alleles are present.
statements.why: It says nothing about which allele spreads, and nothing about strength or fitness.

statements.s: A dominant allele is always the more common one in a population.
statements.why: Frequency and dominance are unrelated; recessive alleles can be essential — most disease resistances breeders chase are recessive.

statements.s: Dominant lethal alleles can persist at high frequency.
statements.why: A dominant lethal cannot persist at all — it kills the individual carrying it.

statements.s: A 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio indicates something non-Mendelian.
statements.why: It is simply incomplete dominance unmasking the genotype ratio instead of collapsing it.

activities.anchor: where S (the selection differential) is how
activities.caption: run the breeder's equation in your head
activities.name: agBreederEstimate

config.prompt: A herd averages 8,000 L per lactation. You select the top cows averaging 9,000 L, so S = 1,000 L. Milk yield has h² ≈ 0.3. How many litres of gain does the breeder's equation predict in the next generation?
config.why: R = 0.3 × 1,000 = 300 L. Most of the selected cows' superiority was environment, and heritability correctly discounts it — which is exactly what the equation buys you.
config.context: 300 litres, against a 1,000-litre head start that was mostly better forage.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this heritability reading
activities.name: agHeritabilitySpot

config.prompt: A student explains heritability to a farmer. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Heritability is a population statistic, not a property of any single animal.
h² of 0.3 means about 30 per cent of each cow's milk yield is genetic.
It is the fraction of the trait's variance attributable to additive genes in that herd and that environment.
It moves: uniform excellent feeding shrinks the environmental share and raises the estimate.
That is part of why genomic selection performs better in well-managed herds.
config.correction: h² of 0.3 means 30 per cent of the trait's VARIANCE in that herd is attributable to additive genes — not 30 per cent of each individual cow's yield.
config.why: Heritability is a variance ratio for a population in an environment. Reading it as a per-animal recipe is the classic error, and it is why the estimate shifts when management becomes more uniform.

activities.caption: drag between the two hazards breeders manage
activities.name: agBreedingCompare

config.prompt: Two opposite effects follow from who mates with whom. Drag the divider.

before.label: inbreeding depression
before.text: Related matings unmask deleterious recessives and cost fitness. This is why breed books cap inbreeding coefficients — and why cheetahs and dog breeds are textbook casualties of a narrowed gene pool.

after.label: heterosis (hybrid vigour)
after.text: Cross two inbred lines and the F1 often outperforms both. Hybrid maize yields 15–20% above open-pollinated varieties, which is why virtually all the maize acreage of the Americas is hybrid.

config.why: The molecular basis of heterosis is still genuinely unsettled — dominance complementation, over-dominance and epigenetic explanations all have evidence — making it one of the oldest open questions in applied genetics.

activities.caption: rank the breeding tools by how much they shortcut time
activities.name: agBreedingToolsOrder

config.prompt: From slowest, most blind selection to fastest, most direct — order these tools:
items: Classical selection on phenotype — six to eight generations of backcrossing, blind for traits only visible at harvest
Marker-assisted selection — a linked marker lets you pick carriers as seedlings
Genomic selection — tens of thousands of SNPs estimate breeding value at birth, roughly halving the dairy generation interval
CRISPR editing — cut at a chosen address and let the cell's own repair make the change
config.why: Each step removes waiting: phenotype to marker to genome-wide prediction to direct edit. Accuracy around 0.5–0.7 from genomic selection, versus ~0.3 from old pedigree records, is what made bull calves need no daughter progeny-testing.

activities.caption: guess the insecticide reduction
activities.name: agGmEstimate

config.prompt: Klümper and Qaim's meta-analysis of 147 studies compared GM and conventional crops. By roughly what percentage did insecticide use fall, on average?
config.why: About 37%, with yields up about 22% on average. Bt cotton in India and China roughly halved spray regimes.
config.context: Better than a third less spray, with a fifth more yield — the average hides wide variation.

activities.caption: decide the governance question
activities.name: agGovernanceBranch

config.root: A new trait is ready. Two paths are open: a transgenic construct carrying a gene from another species, or a CRISPR edit that removes a gene already present in the crop's own gene pool.

start.text: Both reach the same field. The regulatory question is whether they should be assessed the same way.

choices.label: Treat both as one category — GMO — with identical assessment
choices.feedback: That is a legal category, not a biological one: a virus-resistant papaya and a herbicide-tolerant soybean have nothing in common biologically.

choices.label: Assess event-by-event: what protein, expressed where, digested how, with what allergenicity
choices.feedback: This is the assessment logic the safety literature actually supports.

onecategory.text: The single label then carries the risk profile of its most contested member — which is why Golden Rice waited twenty-two years between publication and commercial approval.

eventbyevent.text: The dossier asks about the product, not the technique. That is what allows a virus-resistant papaya and a herbicide-tolerant soybean to be judged on their actual differences.

config.why: GMO is not one technology with one risk profile — it is a legal category. Safety assessment is event-by-event, and the claim that GM DNA behaves differently in the gut is equally misleading: like all DNA in food, it is degraded to nucleotides long before it could reach a consumer's genome.

activities.anchor: 4,000 kg of usable dry matter per hectare
activities.caption: fill the forage budget arithmetic
activities.name: agCarryingCloze

config.text: A temperate pasture yields 4,000 kg of usable dry matter per hectare over the season, and a 500 kg cow eats about 12.5 kg daily — 2.5% of her body weight. That supplies roughly %%0%% cow-days per hectare, and a competent budget deducts %%1%%–50% before that, because residual leaf must remain for regrowth.
config.hint: Divide 4,000 by 12.5 for the raw figure. The deduction range is given in the paragraph — its lower bound.

activities.anchor: the rest period is the active ingredient
activities.caption: bet on why rotation works
activities.name: agRestPredict

config.q: Why does rotational grazing lift forage production 20–50% on the same land?
choices: Because animals moving is itself good for the sward
Because the rest period lets plants rebuild canopy and root reserves
Because fencing excludes pests from the pasture
Because rotational systems always use more fertiliser
config.why: The movement is incidental. A continuously grazed plant is kept at too low a leaf-area index to photosynthesise profitably and drains root carbohydrate rebuilding leaves; a rested plant restores canopy and roots. A rotation with too-short rests performs worse than continuous grazing.

activities.caption: pair each agroecological design with its mechanism
activities.name: agDesignMatch

config.prompt: Each design harvests an interaction a monoculture eliminates. Match design to mechanism:

pairs.right: complementary resource use — deep maize roots beside shallow bean roots

pairs.left: push-pull with Desmodium and Napier grass
pairs.right: repel borers from the stand, trap them in the border, and kill Striga with allelochemicals
drops its leaves during the cropping season — fertilising without shading
fish eat pests and weeds, fertilise the rice, and pay the farmer in protein

config.why: Push-pull roughly doubles maize yields on affected smallholder plots with no synthetic insecticide or herbicide — a designed ecosystem doing the work of three input categories.

activities.caption: compute the land equivalent ratio
activities.name: agLerEstimate

config.prompt: Sole maize yields 6 t/ha; sole beans 2 t/ha. The intercrop yields 4.5 t/ha maize and 1.2 t/ha beans. What is the land equivalent ratio?
config.why: LER = 4.5/6 + 1.2/2 = 0.75 + 0.60 = 1.35. The intercrop needs only about 74% of the land sole crops would require — a 26% land-use efficiency gain.
config.context: 1.35: roughly a third of a hectare saved for every hectare farmed.

activities.caption: true or false — what the ratio actually measures
activities.name: agLerJudge

statements.s: An LER above 1 proves the intercrop beats the sole crops on every count.
statements.why: LER measures land, and only land — not labour, mechanisability or variance.

statements.s: Intercropping is more labour-intensive per hectare than sole cropping.
statements.why: Which is why the practice thrives in labour-rich smallholder systems and struggles in mechanised ones.

statements.s: No combine harvests a mixed stand.
statements.why: Mechanisability is one of the costs LER does not price.

statements.s: The value of an LER gain depends on which resource is actually binding.
statements.why: Land in one system, labour in another — same biology, different institutional answers.

activities.caption: file each argument — spare or share?
activities.name: agSparingBuckets

config.prompt: Land sparing versus land sharing is a genuine empirical fight. File each claim:

items.label: intensify hard and leave the wild un-farmed
forest birds in Ghana and India fare better under high-yield farming with spared land
European farmland birds do better in low-intensity farmland

config.why: Both camps agree yields matter; they disagree about ecological baselines and leakage — does spared land actually stay spared? The defensible synthesis is regional.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this comparison
activities.name: agOrganicSpot

config.prompt: A student compares organic and conventional systems. One line is wrong — find it.
lines: Rothamsted's long-term experiments are the archetype of this evidence.
Organic-matter gains from best practice are real but slow, and carbon saturates.
Cereal yields in organic systems typically run 20–30% ABOVE conventional, paid for by lower input costs.
The premium price compensates for the yield gap, and the stability argument is real.
Agroecology is defined by ecological design, not by certification.
config.correction: Cereal yields in organic systems typically run 20–30% BELOW conventional — the premium price and lower input costs compensate for that gap.
config.why: Many certified-organic farms are input-intensive monocultures, while many agroecological farms use synthetic inputs sparingly. The distinction is which inputs the design makes necessary, not a category ban.

activities.caption: which curve shows regrowth after rest?
activities.name: agRegrowthTrace

config.prompt: Leaf-area index after a paddock is grazed hard. Which curve shows the rested plant rebuilding canopy and root reserves before the next grazing?

curves.label: recovers and levels off once canopy is restored
rises in a straight line with no ceiling

config.why: A rested plant restores canopy and roots, then plateaus. A continuously grazed plant is held at too low an index to photosynthesise profitably and drains root carbohydrate rebuilding leaves.
